analogy.p: Duncan is a gardener who leaves the garden gate open because he believes everyone loves flowers; he plants and waters Macbeth, trusting the soil. Malcolm is the new gardener who fits a lock and checks everyone who enters, so the garden survives. It breaks down because a garden has no politics: Malcolm's locks come with a price, for a lock can also shut out friends.

bullets: Duncan appears in only a handful of scenes (Act 1 Sc 2, 4, 6 and briefly Act 2 Sc 1 in the gift scene reported by Banquo) yet dominates the play through memory: Macbeth and Lady Macbeth are haunted by him to the very end.
Malcolm is the first named heir and the last speaker in the play; the closing speech is his, so the play's final shape is a restored kingdom under a new king.
The two characters are different types of ruler: Duncan trusts too easily, Malcolm trusts too little at first, and the play suggests that a good king needs to learn the right balance.
Both are defined partly by what other characters say about them, which is why the quotation bank for this point includes words spoken by Macbeth, Macduff and Ross.
Neither Duncan nor Malcolm has a soliloquy. Shakespeare reserves interior speech for Macbeth and Lady Macbeth, so the audience reads these two from outside, through action and reputation.

callouts.p: The belief, strongly held by James I, that a monarch is chosen by God, answers only to God, and that to harm or depose a king is a sin against God as well as a crime against the state.

A grade 9 answer on Duncan or Malcolm rarely begins with what happens. Begin with an idea such as "Shakespeare presents Duncan as a sacred figure whose death uncreates Scotland" and then prove it with a quotation and a zoom on one word.
callouts.t: Open with kingship, not with plot

core.h: Why these two characters matter: kingship as the play's moral centre
core.p: Macbeth is not only the story of one man's ambition; it is a study of what happens to a kingdom when the rightful king is murdered. Duncan and Malcolm give the audience the standard against which Macbeth is measured. Duncan represents legitimate, God-ordained kingship at the start; Malcolm represents the hope of its restoration at the end. Because the play was written for a Jacobean audience that believed the king was God's deputy, killing Duncan is not just murder but sacrilege, and Shakespeare saturates the scenes around him with religious and natural imagery to make that clear.

bullets: Act 1 Sc 2: Duncan responds to the news of victory with open praise and honours the Captain's wounds; he does not shout orders or boast, which contrasts with the violent picture of Macbeth in battle.
Act 1 Sc 4: Duncan's reflection on the first Thane of Cawdor, a man in whom he built ‘an absolute trust’, shows that he has already been betrayed once and has not learned from it.
His speech "There's no art / To find the mind's construction in the face" is the most important Duncan line for dramatic irony; Macbeth enters immediately afterwards.
Act 1 Sc 4: naming Malcolm as heir ties kingship to family succession, which is what Macbeth's aside about "a step / On which I must fall down" reacts to.

Act 1 Sc 6: Duncan arrives at Inverness praising the ‘pleasant seat’ of the castle and the sweetness of the air, then thanks his hostess; the gentle blank verse and the courteous plural of royalty show a king at ease with his subjects.
In the gift scene reported in Act 2 Sc 1, Duncan sends a diamond to Lady Macbeth, calling her a ‘most kind hostess’; he is generous to the very couple who plan his death.

callouts.p: Duncan's greatest virtue (trust) is also what exposes him. Shakespeare does not make him foolish; he makes the world around him deceitful, so that goodness itself becomes dangerous. That is one of the play's darkest ideas.

core.h: Duncan in Act 1: the model king
core.p: Duncan is introduced through other people's praise and through his own generosity. In Act 1 Sc 2 he reacts to the bleeding Captain with warmth and gratitude, calling the wounded soldier worthy of care, and rewards Macbeth with the title of the traitor Cawdor. In Act 1 Sc 4 he thanks Macbeth and Banquo, names Malcolm as Prince of Cumberland and tells Macbeth that he has begun to plant him and will labour to make him full of growing. The imagery of planting and growing shows Duncan as a nurturing, almost fatherly king, a gardener of the state; the irony is that he plants the very man who will cut him down.

head: Scene
What Duncan says or does
Effect on the audience
rows: Receives battle news; honours the Captain and Macbeth; gives the Cawdor title to Macbeth
We see a just king who rewards loyalty and punishes treachery
Hears that Cawdor has been executed; thanks Macbeth and Banquo; names Malcolm heir
His trust is touching but dangerously naive; threat to Macbeth's ambition
Arrives at Inverness; admires the castle; honours Lady Macbeth
Peaceful imagery of the martlet and air makes the coming murder more shocking
Sends a gift to Lady Macbeth and sleeps content (reported by Banquo)
He is vulnerable, unguarded and generous at the point of danger
Dead; his body discovered; his sons flee
His absence is felt as a disorder in nature and in the state

bullets: Lady Macbeth cannot do it herself because Duncan "resembled / My father as he slept". The line shows that even the person who has called on spirits to unsex her feels the sanctity of age and kingship.

The contrast of silver and golden colours in Macbeth's speech turns the body into treasure; blood is no longer just horror but something rich and sacred. Macbeth's language here is strangely poetic and may be partly performance, since he is about to kill the grooms and must appear to grieve.

Act 2 Sc 4: Ross and the Old Man report darkness at noon, a falcon killed by a ‘mousing owl’, and Duncan's horses turning wild and eating each other. Natural order mirrors political order: the Great Chain of Being has been broken.

Even after his death Duncan's memory drives the action: Macbeth concedes that Duncan has been so meek and clear in his great office that his virtues will "plead like angels, trumpet-tongued", and later Macbeth envies him: "after life's fitful fever he sleeps well".

In Act 5 Sc 1 Lady Macbeth, sleepwalking, says that no one would have thought the old man to have had "so much blood in him". Her words show that the king's physical, human vulnerability has outlived her ability to ignore it.

callouts.p: Duncan is killed offstage. Describe the effect of that decision (we hear it, we see its aftermath) rather than describing a murder you imagine from a film.
callouts.t: Do not say Duncan ‘dies on stage’

core.p: Duncan is murdered offstage in Act 2 Sc 2, and the choice to keep it unseen matters. The audience hears the crime through Macbeth's panicked report, through Lady Macbeth's practical reaction, and through the knocking, so we experience guilt and consequence rather than spectacle. Duncan's body is then described by Macbeth in Act 2 Sc 3 as having a "silver skin laced with his golden blood", an image of a precious, almost holy object ruined. Macduff calls the murder an act that "hath broke ope / The Lord's anointed temple", which turns the king's body into a church and the killer into a desecrator.

head: Image or detail
Where
What it suggests
rows: "silver skin laced with his golden blood"
The king's body is precious and almost holy; blood becomes treasure and wound together
Regicide as sacrilege; the king is God's house
A lowly creature kills a noble one: reversal of hierarchy
Nature turns unnatural when the king is killed
Duncan returns as a haunting physical presence

bullets: Weave context into an argument: do not write "In 1605 there was a Gunpowder Plot" as a separate sentence. Write instead that, for an audience that had just survived the Gunpowder Plot, Duncan's murder is not only a political event but a sacrilege.
James believed that kings were God's deputies on earth; that is why the play uses religious imagery such as ‘anointed’ and ‘angels’ around Duncan.

The English king Edward (the Confessor), in Act 4 Sc 3, is shown healing the ‘King's Evil’ by touch. James I himself was believed to continue this royal healing practice, so the play implies that a rightful king brings health to the body politic, while a tyrant brings disease.
Banquo was believed to be an ancestor of James. That link makes the survival of Banquo's line, and the stability of the monarchy, a matter of pride for the royal audience.
Be careful with dates and detail: say ‘around 1606’ and ‘James I’, not precise performance dates unless you are certain.

callouts.p: The Elizabethan and Jacobean belief in a divinely ordered hierarchy from God through angels, monarchs, nobles and ordinary people down to animals and plants; to disturb one rank was to disturb all.

Idea + context + effect on this moment. For example: the reference to the Lord's anointed temple reflects the Jacobean belief that a king was God's chosen deputy, so Macduff presents regicide as sacrilege, magnifying Macbeth's guilt.

core.h: Context (AO3): James I, regicide and the Gunpowder Plot
core.p: Macbeth was probably written around 1606 and performed for King James I, who had been king of Scotland as James VI before succeeding Elizabeth I in 1603. James had survived the Gunpowder Plot in 1605, an attempt to blow up Parliament with the king inside it, so an audience was acutely aware of the horror of regicide. James also wrote on kingship and believed in divine right; treason was understood as an offence against God's order. Shakespeare's source, Holinshed's Chronicles, presents a different, less saintly Duncan; Shakespeare chooses to make him virtuous so that Macbeth's crime is as dark as possible and so that the king in the audience is flattered.

bullets: Act 1 Sc 4: Malcolm is named heir and given the title Prince of Cumberland. This public honour is the trigger for Macbeth's aside about the ‘step’ he must ‘fall down’ or ‘o'erleap’.
Act 2 Sc 3: Malcolm's line "To show an unfelt sorrow is an office" shows his shrewdness: he has seen through public grief performed by others.

Donalbain says "There's daggers in men's smiles". The brothers split up to reduce risk, which presents them as pragmatic rather than cowardly, although other characters (Ross, Macduff) are quick to suspect them.

Act 4 Sc 3: In England Malcolm tests Macduff by claiming he is lustful, greedy and without a single kingly virtue, before revealing that these were lies. He does so because ‘Devilish Macbeth’ has tried similar tricks to lure him into Scotland.

Act 5 Sc 4: Malcolm orders every soldier to cut a bough from Birnam Wood to disguise the army's numbers, a clever use of the witches' prophecy; this shows tactical intelligence and turns ‘impossible’ into practical strategy.
Act 5 Sc 8: he becomes king, rewards the thanes with the title of earl, promises to recall exiles and to act "in measure, time and place".

fig.cap: Malcolm's power to act grows through the play; the lowest point is the flight in Act 2 Sc 3, the highest the coronation.

core.p: Malcolm begins as a rescued prince and ends as king. Shakespeare gives him very few early lines, which creates a sense of a young man overshadowed by his father and by Macbeth; his growth is shown by action rather than by speech. In Act 1 Sc 2 he identifies the Captain as the soldier who fought to save him from captivity, so his first act is to give credit to others. In Act 1 Sc 4 he describes the execution of Cawdor, saying that "nothing in his life / Became him like the leaving it", which shows his early skill as a reader of character and his respect for a good death. Then in Act 2 Sc 3 he and his brother Donalbain flee, a decision that saves Malcolm's life but also helps Macbeth to claim that they are guilty.

head: Moment
Malcolm's action
What it shows
rows: Identifies the Captain as the soldier who fought for him
Humility and gratitude; he is young and has been protected
Named Prince of Cumberland; describes Cawdor's death
Heir apparent; observant and morally serious
Distrusts the other lords' grief; flees to England
Caution and survival instinct; suspicion falls on him
Tests Macduff with false vices; later praises Macduff's honesty
Political intelligence, but also an excess of suspicion
Orders the army to carry Birnam boughs
Practical leadership; the prophecy is fulfilled by human action
Accepts the crown, rewards thanes, closes the play
Restored order; faint ambiguity about the new regime

bullets: Malcolm names the "king-becoming graces" (justice, verity, temperance, stableness, bounty, perseverance, mercy, lowliness, devotion, patience, courage, fortitude) and says he has none of them. This list tells us exactly what Shakespeare thinks a king should be.
He fears that Macbeth's agents are trying to lure him back to Scotland and kill him. Malcolm's suspicion is the learned response to the trusting disaster of Duncan.

The scene also contains a moving moment when Ross tells Macduff of the murder of his family; Malcolm urges "Let grief / Convert to anger; blunt not the heart, enrage it", which turns private grief into public action. Macduff's reply, that he must also feel it as a man, keeps the human balance.

Malcolm refers to Macbeth as the tyrant "whose sole name blisters our tongues", linking tyranny to physical pain, and says "Macbeth / Is ripe for shaking", an agricultural metaphor that returns to nature imagery.
The scene also gives the English king Edward as a model: holy, healing and supported by God. It is the moral contrast to Macbeth's Scotland.

callouts.p: Reading 1: a shrewd leader who protects himself and Scotland by testing a possible spy. Reading 2: a ruler whose first instinct is to deceive, hinting that restoration will bring a colder, more political Scotland. A grade 9 response offers both, then decides which the play supports more strongly.

core.h: Malcolm's test of Macduff (Act 4 Sc 3): why it matters
core.p: This long, often cut scene is the play's most important picture of good kingship. Malcolm accuses himself of being lustful, then greedy, then devoid of every royal virtue, and his false confessions are so extreme that the audience feels Macduff's despair at Scotland's future. When Macduff says that such a man is not fit to govern, Malcolm declares that Macduff's honest reaction has proved his loyalty and that he is "yet / Unknown to woman" and has never lied. The scene shows that a king must be able to tell true from false, a skill Duncan lacked, but it also raises the question of whether Malcolm's lies are a dangerous habit in a ruler.

bullets: ‘Dead butcher’ is a blunt, reductive phrase: Malcolm judges Macbeth by his deeds, not by his earlier greatness, which is the opposite of the sympathy the audience may have felt during the soliloquies.
The phrase ‘fiend-like queen’ is the final word on Lady Macbeth and pushes her death into the language of moral judgment, though the audience has seen her breakdown and may feel more complex pity.
By telling us that she "by self and violent hands / Took off her life" the speech reports her suicide in a single line; the contrast with her earlier prominence may feel abrupt.
‘Grace’ is used twice in "by the grace of Grace", linking the new reign to divine approval, the exact opposite of the witches' unholy influence.
Alternative interpretation: Malcolm's calm and the shortness of his speech could be read as a worrying sign that the new regime will be bland or merely political, because it has no poetry of its own.

callouts.p: In a (b) question on kingship or order, the final speech is evidence that Shakespeare restores order, but also that restoration is paid for by deaths and by lost innocence. Say "the cyclical structure" and describe how the play opens in disorder and closes in a controlled public speech.
callouts.t: Use the ending as a structural point

core.h: The closing speech: restoration, or something more complicated?
core.p: The play ends on Malcolm. He thanks the thanes, makes them earls, a new title in Scotland, promises to call home the exiled and to bring forth the agents of Macbeth's tyranny, and describes Macbeth as a ‘dead butcher’ and Lady Macbeth as his ‘fiend-like queen’. He ends by saying that all will be done "by the grace of Grace" and invites everyone to see him crowned at Scone. The tone is orderly, public and formal, in contrast to the chaos of the earlier acts. Structurally the play moves from a chaotic opening in which the witches declare that fair is foul to a closing sense of public, formal order.

bullets: Duncan's death makes Malcolm's survival the main hope for the audience; the two together create a pattern of loss and renewal.

Another foil for Malcolm is Macduff: the older loyal thane who acts from emotion while Malcolm acts from calculation. The tension between them in Act 4 Sc 3 shows that both emotion and strategy are needed.
Another foil for Duncan is Edward of England, who is the wise and holy king that Duncan might have been in a safer world.
Be ready to move from character to theme: Duncan and Malcolm are essential for questions on kingship, loyalty, order and disorder, and appearance and reality.
core.h: Comparing Duncan and Malcolm: foils and contrasts
core.p: Duncan and Malcolm are not copies of each other. Duncan rules by generosity and trust, Malcolm by caution and strategy; Duncan is old and fatherly, Malcolm young and still learning. Both contrast with Macbeth, who rules by fear. Setting them side by side shows Shakespeare's argument that goodness alone is not enough in a deceitful world, and that tyranny can only be ended by a leader who combines virtue with political skill.

bullets: Plan in a short paragraph: thesis, 4 ideas, and a short quotation for each, including one from early, middle and late in the play.
In a Duncan question use the sequence: trust (Act 1), vulnerability (Act 1 Sc 6), death (Act 2), legacy (Act 2 Sc 4 and Act 5).
In a Malcolm question use the sequence: promise (Act 1 Sc 4), flight (Act 2 Sc 3), test (Act 4 Sc 3), command (Act 5 Sc 4), crown (Act 5 Sc 8).
Aim for at least one structural point per paragraph: placement of a scene, contrast with the previous scene, shift of verse to prose, soliloquy versus public speech.
Always say what the writer is doing: "Shakespeare uses the image of ... to suggest that ..." rather than "the quotation shows ...".
Use comparative words such as ‘whereas’, ‘in contrast’ and ‘similarly’ when you move between Duncan, Malcolm and Macbeth.

callouts.p: Only write quotations you are certain of. If you cannot recall the exact words, describe the image instead. A wrong quotation is more damaging than a paraphrase.

core.h: Exam technique: writing about Duncan and Malcolm
core.p: Edexcel Macbeth questions tend to ask about a character or theme in an extract (part a) and then a second question that moves to elsewhere in the play using remembered quotations (part b). The most useful skill is to turn a single quotation into an argument. Choose short, flexible phrases, such as "the Lord's anointed temple" or ‘ripe for shaking’, and zoom in on one word. Remember that AO1 rewards a developed argument, AO2 the analysis of language, form and structure, AO3 the contexts in which Shakespeare wrote, and AO4 (on this question) accurate spelling, punctuation and vocabulary. Check the marks and timings printed on your paper for the exact breakdown.

plan: Duncan as sacred, nurturing king (planting, trust) and the irony that makes him vulnerable.
The murder and its aftermath as sacrilege: ‘anointed temple’, unnatural omens; AO3 divine right and 1605.
Malcolm's flight and the slow acquisition of political skill.
The test of Macduff as a model of a king's need to read people; alternative reading.
The final speech: restored order, ambiguity, structure.
essays.q: Explore how Shakespeare presents ideas about kingship in Macbeth, with reference to Duncan and Malcolm.
essays.text:
Shakespeare presents kingship in Macbeth as something both sacred and dangerously fragile. Duncan embodies the sacred side: a king whose virtue is so complete that it becomes a weakness, and whose murder shatters Scotland. Malcolm embodies the lesson that survival and restoration require something extra, a political intelligence that Duncan never had.

Duncan is introduced as a nurturing, almost agricultural king. When he tells Macbeth "I have begun to plant thee", the horticultural metaphor presents the king as a gardener of his people, and the verb ‘plant’ implies patience and faith in the future. Yet the placement of this speech, immediately after Duncan has admitted there is "no art / To find the mind's construction in the face", turns kindness into irony. He has just spoken of a traitor he trusted, and in the next breath he trusts another. The audience, who have heard Macbeth's aside about the ‘step’ he must ‘o'erleap’, sees that Duncan's generosity is feeding the ambition that will destroy him. Shakespeare therefore makes goodness itself the king's vulnerability, and the fault lies less in Duncan than in a world that can wear a smile like a mask.

The murder is kept offstage, but its meaning is delivered through religious language. Macduff's metaphor of "The Lord's anointed temple" draws on the Jacobean belief in divine right: for an audience watching a play in the reign of James I, soon after the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, regicide was not merely a political crime but an offence against God. The temple image also implies that the king's body is a place of worship, so that to enter and destroy it is desecration. Ross's report of a ‘mousing owl’ killing a falcon extends the point into nature: the Great Chain of Being has been broken, and a lowly bird overturns a noble one just as a thane has overturned a king. Duncan's murder is therefore represented as a cosmic event as much as a human one.

Malcolm's arc answers this disorder, but not easily. Shakespeare presents him first as a young man of promise and then as a fugitive who flees to England after observing that "To show an unfelt sorrow is an office". The flight saves the line of kings, and the aphorism shows an eye for hypocrisy that Duncan lacked. In Act 4 Sc 3 this wariness is tested to its limit when Malcolm accuses himself of every vice before Macduff. On one reading the test is a necessary piece of political education: a king must be able to distinguish an honest friend from a spy. On another it reveals a ruler whose instinct is deceit, hinting that the new Scotland will be colder than the old. Either way, the scene tells the audience which qualities Shakespeare thinks a king needs: the "king-becoming graces" together with realism.

The closing speech completes the shape. Malcolm names Macbeth ‘this dead butcher’ and promises to call home exiles and to act "in measure, time and place", the orderly rhythm of the phrase contrasting with the earlier chaos. He ends with ‘grace’, the theological word that places the new reign under God. Yet restoration comes at a cost; the stage is littered with dead, and the abrupt, formal tone of Malcolm's speech may leave an audience wondering what kind of king will emerge from it.

Shakespeare therefore uses Duncan and Malcolm to argue that kingship demands a double virtue: the sanctity that makes a king a king, and the vigilance that keeps him alive. A Jacobean audience, flattered by the triumph of legitimate kingship yet reminded of treason's reach, is invited to see the Stuart monarchy as the heir of both qualities.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare uses Duncan and Malcolm to suggest that legitimate kingship is both sacred and fragile: goodness alone cannot protect a kingdom, but a ruler who joins virtue to vigilance can restore it.
why: AO1: a conceptual thesis (sacred but fragile; virtue plus vigilance) is sustained through the whole response rather than listing events.
AO2: zooms in on single words and images (‘plant’, ‘anointed temple’, ‘mousing owl’) and comments on structure (placement of Duncan's speech, offstage murder, the closing speech).
AO3: context is woven into the argument (divine right, the Gunpowder Plot, James I) and linked to specific images, not added as a separate paragraph.
Offers alternative readings of Malcolm's test and ending ("on one reading... on another"), which is a clear mark of the top band.
AO4: controlled paragraphs, precise topic sentences and sophisticated vocabulary (‘desecration’, ‘aphorism’, ‘vigilance’).

quotes.a: Duncan reflects on the first Cawdor's betrayal, yet his statement that nobody can read a mind from a face is immediately undercut when Macbeth enters. The abstract nouns ‘art’ and ‘construction’ make hypocrisy sound like architecture, and the line ironically describes Macbeth's own mask. It makes Duncan both wise and blind: he states the truth and then ignores it.
quotes.c: Jacobean fear of treason and hidden plots, heightened after 1605
quotes.q: no art / To find the mind's construction in the face

quotes.a: Duncan's repetition of ‘more’ and the paradox of repayment that cannot be made suggest overflowing generosity, but the language of debt is a trap: Macbeth later wants to pay Duncan in a different coin. The line shows how kingship works through gift and obligation, and how an ambitious subject can resent that obligation.
quotes.c: Feudal ideas of loyalty in exchange for reward
quotes.q: More is thy due than more than all can pay
quotes.t: repetition, paradox, semantic field of debt

quotes.a: The horticultural metaphor presents Duncan as a nurturing king who grows his thanes. It is gentle and organic, which makes it the opposite of Macbeth's later violent vocabulary. A second reading is more ominous: what is planted can also be uprooted, and nature imagery in the play ends by turning against the king.
quotes.c: The king as father and gardener of the state
quotes.q: I have begun to plant thee

quotes.a: The simple, courteous statement and the sweet air that follows create a calm so complete that it feels like the last breath before a storm. Placing this gentle speech after Lady Macbeth's invocation of murder is the play's sharpest dramatic irony, and the adjective ‘pleasant’ is almost grotesquely understated for a place where he will die.
quotes.c: Divine right: a king arrives innocent in a host's house
quotes.q: This castle hath a pleasant seat

quotes.a: Macbeth's own words on Duncan's virtues show how the king's goodness operates as a moral force. Angels are God's messengers and trumpets announce judgment, so Duncan's virtue is imagined as a divine prosecution against his killer. The alliteration of the hard ‘t’ sounds adds a sense of public denunciation.

Macduff's metaphor turns Duncan's body into a sacred building. The adjective ‘anointed’ refers to coronation oil, so the audience hears religious and political horror at once. A temple can be desecrated but not unmade; the image also suggests that the sacredness of the king's body is permanent even after death.
quotes.c: Divine right; Gunpowder Plot (1605) made regicide an urgent horror

quotes.a: Macbeth's rich, ornamental language makes Duncan look like a treasure ruined, and the colours silver and gold suggest royalty. The contrast between this ornate image and the earlier practical bloodiness of the murder suggests that Macbeth is performing grief, or that part of him genuinely feels the loss; both readings keep him complex.
quotes.c: Blood and kingship; blood as lineage
quotes.q: silver skin laced with his golden blood

quotes.a: Lady Macbeth's failure to kill Duncan reveals that her cruelty is not complete. The father image makes regicide also seem like parricide, thus breaking the family and the state in one blow. The conditional ‘had he not’ is ambiguous: it admits that without the resemblance she would have done it.
quotes.c: The king as father of his country
quotes.q: Had he not resembled / My father as he slept

quotes.a: Malcolm's description of Cawdor's death shows a young man who understands both courage and repentance. The paradox that dying is the best act of a life is darkly ironic, because the audience will see Macbeth die defiantly rather than penitently. It also shows that Malcolm is careful about judgment, a skill he uses later.
quotes.c: Jacobean interest in a good death and repentance
quotes.q: Nothing in his life / Became him like the leaving it

quotes.a: The brothers' flight is explained in a single, memorable image of hidden danger. The word ‘daggers’ holds the physical threat and the plural suggests many possible killers. The line is also an epigram of the whole play, in which smiling faces (Lady Macbeth's welcome, Macbeth's feigned loyalty) conceal violence.
quotes.c: Fear of treachery at the Jacobean court

quotes.a: Malcolm's agricultural metaphor treats the tyrant as a fruit near to dropping from a tree. It returns the play to natural imagery and suggests that Macbeth's fall is both inevitable and imminent, and that the heavens are on Scotland's side. The enjambment across ‘Macbeth’ and ‘ripe’ gives the thought momentum.
quotes.c: Providence and the overthrow of tyrants

quotes.a: Malcolm's compressed judgment uses blunt, harsh nouns. ‘Butcher’ reduces a once heroic soldier to a killer of innocents, and the pairing with ‘fiend-like queen’ turns the Macbeths into a diabolical couple, ending the play's tragic sympathy with a political verdict. Some critics find it too neat; the audience has seen more complexity than the label allows.
quotes.c: Providential ending flatters a Stuart king who defeats evil
quotes.q: this dead butcher and his fiend-like queen

summary: Duncan is the sacred, trusting king whose murder breaks the natural and moral order of Scotland; Malcolm is the cautious heir who survives, tests loyalty, and restores order. For Edexcel you must be able to track both characters through the play, explain how Shakespeare shapes them as foils to Macbeth, and link them to Jacobean ideas of kingship (AO3).

terms.d: The belief that a monarch rules by God's authority and cannot be lawfully removed by subjects.
The killing of a king; in Jacobean thought a crime against God as well as the state.
When the audience knows something the character does not, as in Duncan's trust of Macbeth.
A character who contrasts with another to highlight their qualities, such as Malcolm and Macbeth.
The divinely ordered hierarchy of creation, which the murder of the king disrupts.
Nature reflecting human events or emotions, as in the omens after Duncan's death.
A tragic flaw or error; Duncan's misplaced trust is sometimes discussed as a version of this, although the term is more usually applied to Macbeth.
Ritually blessed with oil at coronation, signalling God's choice of the king.
Deliberately ambiguous or misleading speech; relevant to the duplicity Duncan cannot read.
